118 S First StreetThe answer

The answer

You can build four townhomes of about 1,200 sq ft each, or five apartments of about 680 sq ft each. Both are reachable. Neither is automatic.

Five is the ceiling, and it is a hard one

Five homes is not five for now. It is the most the Village code allows on a lot this size, using every reduction the code permits, and the code says "in no event" may those reductions go further. A sixth home would need more land than the lot contains.

Ten is not possible

Ten homes would need 22,680 sq ft of land even after every reduction available. This lot is 12,320 sq ft. The site is a little over half the size it would have to be. The figure of ten came from the minimum value a software field would accept, not from anything about this property, and it should not be carried forward.

One thing has to be settled before you spend money on design

To get more than one home here, the Village has to approve your project as a planned development, and when it does that it decides which of its existing zoning districts your project is most similar to. One answer gives you five homes. The other gives you one. Nothing else in this report moves the number as far.

There is a formal, deliberately cheap step that exists to settle exactly this before drawings are commissioned. Take it first. It has its own page later in this document.

118 S First StreetHow the limit works

How the limit works

The town does not cap how many homes you build. It caps how little land each home is allowed to sit on. Think of it as an assigned parking space, but for a house. Divide the lot by that number and you have your answer.

12,320 sq ft
The land you have. That is the whole of it, and it is fixed.
Land required under each homeWhere that number comes from12,320 divided by itHomes
2,800 sq ftThe normal rule for a two-bedroom home4.44
2,268 sq ftThe same rule cut by 20 percent, through a special approval5.435
2,268 sq ft, six times overSix homes would need 13,608 sq ft of land-Will not fit

Six homes fall short by 1,288 sq ft of land. There is no version of the rules that closes that gap. Smaller one-bedroom homes do not close it either: their requirement is 2,106 sq ft each, and 12,320 divided by that is 5.85, which still rounds down to five.

Stacking homes does not help

The rule measures land, not building. Two floors sit on exactly the same ground as one, so adding a storey changes nothing about how many homes the lot can carry.

Removing the space between homes does not help either

In the four-home layout the homes are already attached, sharing walls with no gap between them. Four homes at 19.04 ft across the 76.16 ft of usable width comes to 76.16 ft exactly. There is nothing left between them to take out.

About that 20 percent

The discount comes in two halves. The second half is only available because the parking sits inside the building, which is why both layouts here put the cars in garages. Whether the Village accepts an attached garage as qualifying is an open question, and the fifth home depends on the answer.

118 S First StreetHow big the homes can be

How big the homes can be

There is a second cap, and it works on space rather than on count. Add up every finished square foot, in every home, on every floor. That total may not exceed 4,805 sq ft.

4,805 sq ft
Total finished space allowed across the whole project. That is 39 percent of the lot, which is the most the special approval route permits.

The whole trade is one division:

If you build4,805 divided bySpace per homeWhat that gives you
4 townhomes4about 1,201 sq ftA two-bedroom home
5 apartments5about 961 sq ftBefore parking and stairs come out of it

Fewer bigger homes, or more smaller ones. That is the entire choice.

In an apartment building, the parking eats into it

The five indoor parking bays and the shared lobby and stairs all count inside that same 4,805 sq ft: roughly 1,100 sq ft of garage, and roughly 300 sq ft of lobby and stairs. What is left to live in is about 3,405 sq ft, which is about 680 sq ft per home. The town's minimum for a one-bedroom home is 650 sq ft, so 680 clears it.

A hard finding, not a caution

Five two-bedroom apartments cannot be delivered here. The minimum size for a two-bedroom home is 850 sq ft. Five of those, plus the garages and the shared space, needs about 5,650 sq ft. That is about 46 percent of the lot, or about 42 percent counting the most generous garage allowance the code offers. The cap is 39 percent. At five homes, the homes have to be one-bedroom.

Four two-bedroom apartments do fit, at about 4,580 sq ft, but dropping to four gives up the "five or more homes" definition that is the apartment scheme's whole advantage on the question that decides everything.

A third cap, on how much ground is covered by building, does not bite: no more than 25 percent of the lot may be built on, and both layouts here sit at 19.5 percent.

Sections behind this page: 11-18-3C1, the floor area ceiling. 11-18-3B, parcel coverage. 11-7H-1C, minimum floor area per dwelling unit.

The site, in plain words

0.28 acres. About 96 ft wide along the street and about 128 ft deep.

It fronts 1st Street only, a small street owned by the Village. It does not front Lake Street, which is US Route 20 and is about 448 ft away. That is good news: because your street belongs to the Village and not the State, the driveway does not need a State highway permit.

Not in a flood zone, and no wetlands on the parcel.

The soil holds water and the water table is shallow, at 2.5 ft. That matters for anything buried, and the stormwater tank is buried. The tank goes underground beneath the back yard, and the yard above it stays usable; but whether a buried tank works here at all needs a soils investigation first.

The parcel is currently carried as tax exempt at zero assessed value on the county roll. Under your ownership it goes onto the tax rolls. No tax figure can be quoted, because no assessed value exists yet to quote.

118 S First StreetThe one thing that decides everything

The one thing that decides everything

One decision, made by the Village Board, is worth four of your five homes. Settle it before you commission a single drawing.

The route to more than one home on this lot is a planned development, which is an approval that lets the Village set the rules for your project instead of applying the standard ones. When it does that, it has to decide which of its existing zoning districts your project is most similar in nature and function to, and it takes the numbers from there. Two districts are in play, and they are far apart.

If the Board says R-4
5 homes
The multiple-family district. 2,800 sq ft of land per home, reduced to 2,268 sq ft. The whole of this report holds.
If the Board says R-3
1 home
The district that names row houses and town houses. 8,000 sq ft of land per home, reduced to 6,400 sq ft. The lot carries one.

There is a step that exists to settle this first

Before you apply for anything, the Planning and Zoning Commission approves a tentative plan in principle. The code says the point of it is to let you get the Commission's advice before you incur the expense of a plan. That is the moment to put the district question on the table, and it is a great deal cheaper than finding out after the drawings are paid for.

One thing to know going in: the written consent of every property owner within the development has to be on file with the Village before the Commission will even begin studying a tentative plan.

Why the apartment option is the stronger card here

The multiple-family district's own definition of what it permits is a building containing five or more homes. A five-unit apartment building is literally that, so you are not arguing the point, you are handing the Board the answer. A row of townhomes does the opposite: it matches the other district's own words for row and town houses, and that district carries 8,000 sq ft of land per home.

118 S First StreetWhat to do, in order

What you have to do, in order

  1. Get the zoning confirmed in writing. Ask the Village to confirm the base district is R-2, that the Old Town overlay applies, and what the "SP" notation and ordinance 79-53 on the zoning map attach to this parcel.
  2. Sit down with Village staff before you draw anything. That means the Village Planner and the Village Engineer, because no permit can be issued until both of them have approved a site plan.
  3. Take the informal step that settles the district question. The Planning and Zoning Commission approves a tentative plan in principle before any application is filed. Written consent of every property owner within the development must be on file first.
  4. File the formal application for a planned development special use. The submittal list is long and includes a written list of every exception you are asking for.
  5. Public hearing. The Planning and Zoning Commission holds it, then reports and recommends to the Village Board.
  6. Village Board approval. A written agreement of restrictions is signed with the final plan. After that, nothing about the plan changes without the Board's authorisation.
  7. Permits. Once the Board approves the final plan, the building and zoning official issues them. Separately, the project has to satisfy the DuPage County stormwater rules, which are administered county-wide.

Nobody can tell you how long this takes

This report will not guess. The section of the code that sets the public notice period and the hearing schedule could not be obtained. Ask the Village for it, together with the current meeting calendar and filing deadlines for the Commission and the Board. Those meeting cycles are what actually set your calendar.

The only two hard deadlines, and both start after approval

Approval of each unit of the development is good for 18 months from the date the final plan is approved. And if construction has not started within 18 months of that same date, the permits are void and the project has to be resubmitted and reapproved from the beginning. The Village Board can extend that on a showing of good and sufficient cause.

Neither of these is a processing time. They are clocks that start once you already have your approval.

118 S First StreetWhat could still change the answer

What could still change the answer

Everything here is unresolved today. The first two move the number of homes.

Settle these first
  • Which district the Village Board picks R-4 gives you five homes. R-3 gives you one. The largest single risk in the analysis.
  • A boundary survey Every dimension here comes from county mapping. The lot beats the 12,000 sq ft minimum for a single house by only 320 sq ft, so a survey measuring slightly less matters. The width of 1st Street is derived too, not platted.
Before you rely on the design
  • Whether an attached garage earns the second discount Half of the 20 percent land reduction depends on parking being inside the building, so the fifth home turns on the Village agreeing that an attached garage counts.
  • The Old Town Plan The design document your project is judged against. It has not been reviewed, and could shape the look, the layout, or both.
  • Soil and water table The soil holds water and the water table is 2.5 ft down, both adverse for a buried stormwater tank. Get a soils investigation before the design relies on one.
  • Fire access One point of access for emergency vehicles, where two are commonly required. Confirm with the Bloomingdale Fire Protection District before the layout is fixed.
  • Utilities Water, sanitary and storm service have not been established, and the assessor record lists no sanitary district.
  • How the parking is counted Whether a garage space and the driveway in front of it both count, and whether the guest requirement rounds up, are unresolved.
Before you close the numbers
  • Property taxes Exempt at zero assessed value today, and reassessed onto the tax rolls under your ownership.
  • What is on the site now Whether anything stands on the parcel, and what demolition would involve, has not been established.

PLAN NOTES
  1. Base district R-2 Single-Family Residence with the OTP Old Town Preservation overlay. Bulk and height are taken from the underlying district as directed by 11-11-4A; the bulk table is 11-7D-1.
  2. Option 1 is a planned development special use under Title 11 Chapter 18, an expressly permitted special use in the Old Town district per 11-11-4D5. Relief sought: floor area ratio raised from 0.30 to 0.39, the chapter ceiling under 11-18-3C1; density under 11-18-3C2; and lot width. Parcel coverage 19.5 percent, within the 25 percent cap at 11-18-3B.
  3. One 24 ft curb cut, four private driveways. 11-13-4-2 limits a driveway across public property in a residential use area to 36 ft in width, exclusive of curb returns. A single 24 ft cut is clearly within that limit; four separate 12 ft aprons cut directly to the street would total 48 ft.
  4. Fencing on the First Street frontage is picket style, constructed of wood, or equivalent material approved by the Building Commissioner, per 11-11-8A.
  5. Exterior colours per 11-11-7: Benjamin Moore historical color selection or approved equivalent. Exterior painting requires a permit.
  6. Underground stormwater tank. The tank is below grade and occupies no surface area. It does not reduce open space or usable yard, and the ground above it remains yard. It sits within the rear yard, which is already required to remain open, so it displaces nothing. The only real constraint is that no building may sit on top of it. The extent shown is indicative. Hydrologic soil group C soils with a water table at 2.5 ft remain adverse for a buried structure; a geotechnical investigation is required before underground detention is relied upon.
  7. Guest space is located at the south terminus of the drive aisle. Whether a garage space and an apron each count toward the parking requirement is not established, and the location of the guest space relative to the side yard is to be confirmed with the Village. See "What could still change the answer" in the body of this report.
  8. Right of way width shown is approximate, derived from the gap between opposing cadastral parcel edges. It is not a platted dimension. See "What could still change the answer" in the body of this report.
  9. Single point of vehicular access shown. Confirm fire apparatus access requirements with the Bloomingdale Fire Protection District. See "What could still change the answer" in the body of this report.
  10. No permit issues until the Village Planner and the Village Engineer approve the site plan, per 11-13-3.
